extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, political communication researchers, graduate students in communication, and journalists interested in empirical content analysis and press–state theory
extracted.subtask_description: Content-analysis methodology and theoretical criteria for measuring the frequency, source, and direction of opinions in newspaper news stories and editorials (case study of New York Times coverage of Nicaragua, 1983–1986). Includes sampling, coding, measurement, and analytic-choice rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing hypothesis (norm for coverage selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists implicitly answer what, how much, and whose opinion to cover by looking to 'official' conflict or opposition levels within the government — i.e., press opinion is 'indexed' to the range of consequential institutional debate and opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The indexing norm predicts that editorial and news opinion will rise and fall with levels of institutional (primarily congressional) opposition. The text frames indexing as explaining how journalists choose whose views to present and suggests it operates especially when official conflict is pronounced. Use this as a theoretical lens for interpreting concordance between news-page official-opposition reporting and editorial/op-ed page opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling frame: use of New York Times Index (date-restricted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample consisted of all news articles and editorials indexed under 'Nicaragua' in the New York Times Index between January 1, 1983 and October 15, 1986, supplemented by Lexis/Nexis searches to retrieve items (notably polls) excluded from the Index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: NYT chosen because it is an exemplar of journalistic norms, a cue-setter for other media, and a 'keeper of the nation’s ongoing historical record.' Limitations: the Index omitted some opinion polls, so supplementary text searches are necessary. When possible, document and correct for Index omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis: voiced opinions in news and editorials
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the frequency, direction, and source of all opinions voiced in news stories and in editorial/op-ed content during the sampled period; news and editorial content analyzed separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count each distinct voiced opinion as a unit. Articles that document contesting positions should be coded as multiple voices (e.g., an article documenting a battle between President Reagan and House Speaker O’Neill is double-coded). Maintain separate tallies for news-page voiced opinions and editorial/op-ed voiced opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary decision: whether an opinion was voiced
rubrics_metrics.description: Coders first judged whether an opinion was voiced in each abstract/article; this mechanical task yielded 98% agreement and separated non-opinionated ('descriptive') items from opinionated ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve ambiguous cases (e.g., passing references to domestic debates in field reports) by coder discussion. Keep the initial coding task simple to maximize intercoder agreement; record clerical errors separately and correct them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding dimensions: voice and valence
rubrics_metrics.description: If an opinion was voiced, coders judged who voiced it (voice) and the direction of the opinion (valence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valence coding uses symbols: + (supportive of administration contra policy), - (opposed), and ± (ambivalent/divided). Provide clear examples in the codebook (e.g., when a report characterizes a House vote as a 'major policy victory' code Congress as voice and valence as +). Keep categories simple to improve intercoder reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of voice (source classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voices were classified into categories: editorial and op-ed, administration source, congressional source, judicial source, popular (nongovernmental) source including interest groups and polls, and foreign opinion from U.S. allies. Sandinista and contra voices were assigned 'no valence'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about category boundaries. Example handling: speeches by presidents, statements by committees, poll references, interest-group statements each get appropriate voice codes. Sandinista/contra opinions are 'canceled out' (no valence) when the focus is U.S. domestic policy processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Sandinista and contra voices (no valence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions from Sandinistas and contras were assigned 'no valence' codes and effectively canceled out in analyses aimed at evaluating domestic U.S. policy supportability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the study focused on domestic U.S. policy processes and comparability of domestic actors; if opposing foreign actors are balanced in number, neutral coding prevents distortion of domestic-opinion measures. Document such decisions and their expected impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting rule: equal weight for all coded voices
rubrics_metrics.description: For the primary evaluation, all coded voices were weighted the same — e.g., President Reagan counted the same as an undersecretary, a poll, or a grassroots statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simplifies analysis and keeps intercoder reliability high but has implications: prominence and authority differences are ignored. The authors note that alternate weighting schemes could be explored for more sophisticated analyses; document rationale if deviating from equal-weight approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding of institutional actions as voices (e.g., roll-call votes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional actions were coded as single 'voices' when summarized in the Times in terms of policy outcomes (e.g., a Senate roll call summarized as a 'victory' or 'loss' was coded as one voice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat summarized institutional outcomes as voices when the article frames them as policy-significant events. Ensure consistency: if a vote is reported with multiple positions, decide whether to code it as a single aggregated voice or multiple voices per position, and document the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-voice articles: code each position separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles describing different policy positions were coded as multiple voices (e.g., an article documenting a battle between president and speaker coded as both 'administration voice' and 'congressional voice').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows capture of contested reporting and prevents undercounting of opposing perspectives. Maintain rules for when to split vs. aggregate within a single article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercoder reliability principle: simplicity for reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping codes simple paid off in high intercoder reliability (.94 for voice and valence on 1,177 cases). Most disagreements were clerical or marginal valence differences resolved by mutual agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design codebooks and training to minimize subjective judgment. Expect some valence interpretation disputes; resolve through coder discussion and document reconciliation steps. Report intercoder reliability statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal partitioning: analysis intervals tied to key policy events
rubrics_metrics.description: The three-year period was broken into 17 intervals corresponding to episodes climaxed by key policy votes in Congress to observe variation during times with and without congressional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting intervals around institutional actions allows analysis of indexing effects across policy-activity states. But note that a small number of intervals (n=17) advises caution in relying heavily on statistical inference; emphasize structural patterns and graphical displays as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of editorial opposition: net editorial opposition vs total opposition voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Two measures used: (1) net editorial opposition (con editorials/op-eds minus pro editorials/op-eds) — used for conceptual/theoretical reasons and stability with small counts; (2) total opposition voices as a percent of all opinions — produced an even stronger indexing coefficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose net measure when editorial numbers are small and when departures from expected balance are theoretically meaningful to readers; cross-check with total-voices measure. Report correlations between measures to show robustness (authors reported r = .63 using net, r = .76 using total op-ed opposition voices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic emphasis: structural/graphical patterns over heavy statistical reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of small number of intervals and the exploratory nature, the analysis emphasizes structural and graphically visible patterns; statistics (e.g., Pearson correlations) are reported for key patterns but interpreted cautiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build confidence by layering consistent patterns across multiple indicators and by visual confirmation (graphs) rather than overrelying on p-values from small-N series. When using correlations, report them but explain limitations due to temporal/interval sample size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for index limitations (polls often excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: The New York Times Index regularly omitted a substantial percentage of opinion polls on the issue; these had to be retrieved separately via Lexis/Nexis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on secondary indexes, assess what types of items may be systematically excluded and supplement with full-text database searches. Note the potential bias introduced by Index omissions in interpreting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of 'congressional opposition' measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional opposition was calculated as the number of voices, votes, and journalistic characterizations of opposition from members and voting blocs in Congress as a percent of the total of all opinions expressed in the New York Times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate multiple forms of congressional opposition (statements, votes, characterizations) into a single percent measure against all voiced opinions to capture the magnitude of official institutional opposition. Clearly define inclusion rules for what counts as congressional opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of domain variance in indexing applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexing may vary across issue areas; it is expected to operate most consistently in military decisions, foreign affairs, trade, and macroeconomic policy — areas important to corporate interests and state power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the indexing hypothesis to other topics, consider institutional salience and corporate/state stakes; anticipate weaker indexing when clean opinion divisions among institutional power blocs are absent or when the issue is peripheral to dominant interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative recommendation: press independence for democratic accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: To break the cycle of indexed news that compresses public opinion to institutional debate, a return to an independent press willing to exercise independent judgment is recommended; change likely requires external shocks (market decline, public loss of confidence, societal shifts) or professional reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is prescriptive rather than methodological: use empirical findings to argue for institutional reforms, training, and incentives that would empower journalists to report beyond institutional indexing. When proposing reforms, specify plausible catalysts and pathways (corporate change, journalism education, grassroots pressure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and transparency: report coding rules, examples, and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide concrete illustrative index entries and examples to convey the coding scheme's flavor and make the coding tasks straightforward; record clerical errors and reconciliation procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include codebook excerpts, sample coded items, and specifics (e.g., sample index text and its assigned code) so readers can assess coding validity. Transparency enhances credibility and allows replication or reanalysis.
